title: Stop Trying to Prove They Used AI
author: Doan Winkel
source: How to Teach With AI (howtoteachwithai.substack.com), August 12, 2026
summary: Doan Winkel's How to Teach With AI newsletter argues that teachers chasing "proof" a student used AI are fighting a battle they cannot win -- AI detectors flag international and careful student writers as readily as they flag AI-generated text, and building a case consumes the hour that could instead go toward the only question that actually matters: can the student explain the thinking behind their own work? His alternative is a "five-minute defense" built into every major assignment from day one: after submission, a randomly selected handful of students (never just the suspected ones) walk the teacher through two decisions they made in the work, a design that reads as routine quality-checking rather than accusation. He supplies a copy-paste AI prompt teachers can run against their own assignment and rubric to generate six discriminating oral-defense questions plus a non-accusatory opening script for when a student's answers don't hold up, and recommends piloting the check on a low-stakes early assignment so it reads as a stated classroom norm rather than a trap introduced once suspicion arises later in the semester.
points: Winkel's central claim is that AI-detection tools operate at a courtroom standard of proof teachers don't need and can't reliably meet, while a five-minute oral defense exposes the same problem in under two minutes without accusing anyone.

The routine's key design choice is random selection of students for the post-assignment conversation, not just the ones a teacher suspects -- which is what keeps the check from reading as an accusation and lets students who did the work actually enjoy it.

He provides a ready-to-use AI prompt that generates both six discriminating oral-defense questions (about decisions and tradeoffs, never definitions) and a non-accusatory 120-word opening script for the moment a student's answers don't hold up.

His practical rollout advice is to pilot the check on the very first small assignment, when stakes are low, because introducing it later in the semester -- once a teacher already suspects a specific student -- reads as a trap rather than a stated classroom norm.
quotes: So you run a paragraph through a detector, which says 87%, which means nothing, because it says something similar about the international student who writes carefully and the honors kid who over-edits.

Proof is a courtroom standard. You aren't running a courtroom, and every hour you spend building a case is an hour you're not spending on the only question that matters: can this student explain the thinking in this work?
Someone who did the thinking can talk about it. Someone who didn't will stall inside ninety seconds. That gap shows up without a detector, without an accusation, and without a hearing.

Random selection is the whole design. Nobody gets singled out, so the conversation is never an accusation, and the students who did the work tend to enjoy it. The version that fails is the one where you only pull the students you suspect.

It cannot accuse, it cannot mention AI in the first thirty seconds, and it has to end with a specific next step the student can take. Under 120 words, written as words I would say out loud, not as a policy paragraph.

The September version of you is holding a paper that is too clean and has two options: a fight you can't win, or a B minus and a shrug. The August version of you has six questions in a document and a script for the hard part, and needs neither.
